title: What is Feature Engineering
abstract:
The map for the next twenty-two topics. Feature engineering is the process of
using domain knowledge to extract features from raw data so that ML
algorithms perform better. It splits into four branches — transformation,
construction, selection and extraction — and this document defines each,
shows what each does to the data matrix, explains why this stage matters more
than algorithm choice (the Bayes-error argument), and states the one rule that
governs every technique in Part II: fit on train, transform both.

blocks.t: The Definition
From the notes

Feature Engineering is the process of using domain knowledge to extract
features from raw data. These features can be used to improve the performance of
machine learning algorithms.
Two words in that sentence carry the weight.

"Domain knowledge" — this is the part a library cannot do for you.
Knowing that a transaction $400$ km from the previous one, six minutes later, is
physically impossible and therefore suspicious is domain knowledge. No amount of
hyperparameter tuning discovers it.

"Raw data" — what you receive is almost never in the form an
algorithm can use. Dates arrive as strings, categories as text, quantities on
wildly different scales, and values simply missing.
The Four Branches

blocks.cap:
The taxonomy from the notes. Transformation has four sub-topics of its
 own; those four occupy Topics 13–30 of this course.

The same four branches described by their effect on the data matrix.
 This is the fastest way to keep them straight: transformation changes values,
 construction adds columns, selection removes columns, extraction replaces many
 columns with a few new ones.

blocks.t: 1. Feature Transformation

Changing the values in existing columns so the algorithm can use them.
Four sub-topics, exactly as the notes list them:

head: Sub-topic
What it does
Topics
rows: Either remove or fill missing values — replace by mean, median, or most frequent category
Convert text categories to numbers, e.g. One-Hot Encoding
Detect and treat extreme values; models fit much better once outliers are handled
Bring all values onto a common scale so no feature dominates

blocks.t: 2. Feature Construction
From the notes

Create a new column manually using domain knowledge — for example, a
new column formed by adding two existing columns.

This is where domain expertise converts directly into accuracy. Covered fully in
Topic 31. A few real examples:

head: Constructed feature
Why it beats the raw columns
rows: The ratio is what medicine cares about, not either number alone
Survival on the Titanic depends on group size, not on two separate counts
Comparable across cities in a way that raw price is not
Converts an absolute timestamp into a recency signal

blocks.t: 3. Feature Selection
From the notes

Selecting the features useful for the model. The speed of the model
increases.

You keep a subset of the original columns and discard the rest. The
columns that survive are unchanged and still interpretable — this is the key
difference from extraction.

head: Family
How it decides
Examples
rows: Correlation, chi-square, mutual information, variance threshold

blocks.t:
Benefits: faster training and inference, less overfitting, smaller artefacts,
and a model a human can still read.
4. Feature Extraction
From the notes

Examples: PCA (Principal Component Analysis), LDA. This is done
by the system, not manually.

Extraction combines many columns into a smaller number of new
ones. The notes' own example (Topic 02): if you have number of rooms and
number of bathrooms, dimensionality reduction can merge them into a single
new column, roughly "square footage". Covered in Topics 32–33.
Selection vs extraction — the distinction that gets tested

head: Selection
Extraction
rows: Keeps a subset of original columns

blocks.t: Why This Stage Matters Most
The Bayes-error argument, restated
For a fixed feature set $X$, the lowest error achievable by any model is
R^{*}(X)=\mathbb{E}_X \left[1-\max_c P(Y=c\mid X)\right].

$R^*$ depends on the joint distribution of $(X,Y)$, not on the algorithm.
Switching from a random forest to XGBoost moves you closer to $R^*(X)$; it
cannot move $R^*(X)$ itself. Only changing $X$ — through construction,
transformation or extraction — lowers the floor. That is the formal content
of the saying "better features beat better algorithms".

This is why Part II is 22 of the 82 topics in this course, and why the effort
distribution in Topic 07 puts feature work at roughly 60% of a project.
The One Rule That Governs Every Technique in Part II
Fit on train, transform on both — the notes state this repeatedly
Every technique in the next 21 topics learns parameters from data:

head: Technique
What it learns and must not relearn on test
rows: the mean $\bar x$ and standard deviation $\sigma$

blocks.t:
All of these must be computed on the training set only and then
applied to the test set. Recomputing them on test leaks information and
inflates your metrics. In scikit-learn: fit_transform() on train,
transform() on test — never fit anything on test.
Which is why Pipelines exist

Doing this by hand across ten transformers is error-prone, and the error is
silent. The Pipeline and ColumnTransformer objects (Topics 16–17)
enforce the rule structurally: one object holds every fitted parameter, and the
identical object is used in production.
Ordering: What Comes Before What
The order of operations is not arbitrary, and getting it wrong is a common bug.

head: Step
Why here
rows: Everything after this must be fitted on train only
Most later steps cannot run with NaNs
Because they distort the scaling statistics computed next

blocks.t: The notes are explicit about step 6

"Feature scaling is generally the last thing that we do in the FE
pipeline, right before feeding the data to the model." Scaling before outlier
removal means the outliers set the scale; scaling before encoding means you have
nothing numeric to scale.
Code: The Four Branches in One Script

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, mutual_info_classif
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 3000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "age":        rng.integers(18, 70, n).astype(float),
    "income":     rng.lognormal(10.5, .6, n),
    "tenure_d":   rng.integers(1, 2000, n).astype(float),
    "n_products": rng.poisson(2, n).astype(float),
    "city":       rng.choice(["mumbai", "delhi", "pune", "kochi"], n),
    "plan":       rng.choice(["basic", "premium"], n),
})
df.loc[rng.random(n) < .08, "income"] = np.nan
df["y"] = (0.00002 * df.income.fillna(df.income.median())
           + 0.02 * df.n_products - 0.001 * df.tenure_d
           + rng.normal(0, .4, n) > 0.6).astype(int)

X, y = df.drop(columns="y"), df["y"]
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25,
                                          stratify=y, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# BRANCH 2 -- FEATURE CONSTRUCTION  (manual, needs domain knowledge)
# =====================================================================
def construct(d: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    d = d.copy()
    d["income_per_product"] = d.income / d.n_products.replace(0, np.nan)
    d["tenure_years"]       = d.tenure_d / 365.0
    d["income_per_year"]    = d.income / d.tenure_years.clip(lower=.1)
    d["is_new"]             = (d.tenure_d < 90).astype(int)
    return d
# A library will never invent income_per_product. That is the point.

X_tr, X_te = construct(X_tr), construct(X_te)
num = X_tr.select_dtypes("number").columns.tolist()
cat = X_tr.select_dtypes("object").columns.tolist()

# =====================================================================
# BRANCH 1 -- FEATURE TRANSFORMATION  (imputation, encoding, scaling)
# =====================================================================
transform = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),   # missing value imputation
        ("scale",  StandardScaler()),                   # feature scaling -- LAST
    ]), num),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="first"), cat),
])                                                      # categorical handling

# =====================================================================
# BRANCH 3 -- FEATURE SELECTION   (keep a SUBSET of the original columns)
# =====================================================================
select = SelectKBest(score_func=mutual_info_classif, k=8)

# =====================================================================
# BRANCH 4 -- FEATURE EXTRACTION  (create NEW columns from combinations)
# =====================================================================
extract = PCA(n_components=5)

# =====================================================================
# COMPARE THE FOUR PIPELINES
# =====================================================================
variants = {
    "transform only":            Pipeline([("t", transform),
                                           ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]),
    "transform + selection":     Pipeline([("t", transform), ("s", select),
                                           ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]),
    "transform + extraction":    Pipeline([("t", transform), ("e", extract),
                                           ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]),
}
for name, pipe in variants.items():
    s = cross_val_score(pipe, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
    print(f"{name:26s} cv auc {s.mean():.4f} +/- {s.std():.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# THE RULE: fit on TRAIN, transform BOTH
# =====================================================================
best = variants["transform + selection"]
best.fit(X_tr, y_tr)          # every statistic below is learned from TRAIN only
print("test auc:", best.score(X_te, y_te))

learned = best.named_steps["t"].named_transformers_
print("medians learned from train:",
      learned["num"].named_steps["impute"].statistics_.round(1))
print("means learned from train:",
      learned["num"].named_steps["scale"].mean_.round(1))
print("categories learned from train:", learned["cat"].categories_)
# On X_te these values are REUSED, never recomputed. That is what prevents leakage.

# WHAT NOT TO DO -- the leak, in one line:
#   X_all_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(pd.concat([X_tr, X_te]))
# The mean now contains test information, and your metric is optimistic.

# =====================================================================
# SELECTION vs EXTRACTION -- interpretability, made concrete
# =====================================================================
sel_pipe = variants["transform + selection"].fit(X_tr, y_tr)
names = sel_pipe.named_steps["t"].get_feature_names_out()
kept  = names[sel_pipe.named_steps["s"].get_support()]
print("SELECTION kept real columns:", kept[:5])
# ['num__income' 'num__n_products' ...]  -- still human-readable

ext_pipe = variants["transform + extraction"].fit(X_tr, y_tr)
pca = ext_pipe.named_steps["e"]
print("EXTRACTION built PC1 as a mixture of everything:",
      dict(zip(names[:4], pca.components_[0][:4].round(2))))
# {'num__age': 0.11, 'num__income': 0.63, ...}  -- no longer interpretable
print("variance retained by 5 components:",
      pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum().round(3))
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Feature engineering = using domain knowledge to extract
 features from raw data so that ML algorithms perform better.

Transformation — change values in existing columns.
 Four sub-topics: missing value imputation, handling categorical
 features, outlier detection, feature scaling.

Construction — create new columns manually using
 domain knowledge.

Selection — keep the useful columns; model speed
 increases.

Selection keeps original columns and stays interpretable;
 extraction builds new synthetic ones and does not.

Feature work sets the Bayes error — the floor no algorithm can
 beat. This is why it matters more than algorithm choice.

Order: split $\to$ clean $\to$ impute $\to$ outliers $\to$
 construct $\to$ encode $\to$ scale last $\to$ select/extract.

The rule for all of Part II: every transformer is
 fitted on train only and applied to test.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Difference between feature selection and feature extraction?

Selection keeps a subset of the original columns, so the survivors remain
interpretable. Extraction creates new columns as combinations of the originals
(PCA components), which usually retains more information in fewer dimensions but
sacrifices interpretability.
Q. Why does feature engineering matter more than picking an algorithm?

Q. Give an example of feature construction that a library could never do
for you.

For fraud: implied_speed = distance_from_last_txn /
time_since_last_txn. A value of $900$ km/h means the same card was used in
two cities within an impossible interval. Neither raw column reveals this; the
ratio does. It requires knowing that people cannot teleport.
Q. Should you scale before or after handling outliers?

After. Outliers distort the mean and standard deviation, so scaling first means
the outliers determine everybody else's scaled values. Scaling is the last step
before the model.
Q. What breaks if you fit the scaler on the full dataset?

The training set gains information about the test distribution — the mean and
standard deviation encode it. Validation scores become optimistic and production
performance is worse than reported. Fit on train, transform both.
